title: Take several permits or none

blocks.text: `acquire(n)` is not `n` calls to `acquire()`. The page: it waits until all `n` permits are free **at the same moment** and takes them together, so a waiting thread never sits on a partial set that another thread needs; and it is either fully acquired or not at all, even when interrupted. `tryAcquire(n)` is the same without waiting. The page's `MultiPermitExample` shows the risky one-at-a-time version.
Write `Leases`, which hands out I/O buffers from a fixed stock, backed by a `Semaphore`:

items: `void lease(int n)` waits until `n` buffers are free and takes them all at once. A caller interrupted while it waits leaves with `InterruptedException` and holds nothing.
`boolean tryLease(int n)` takes `n` buffers only if all `n` are free right now, and otherwise takes **none** and returns `false`.
`int available()` is the number of free buffers.

blocks.text: The tests never race two callers against each other inside `tryLease`, so a check followed by a separate take, or taking permits one by one and handing them back on failure, gives the same answers here. Both are the page's pitfalls under contention; the single `tryAcquire(n)` is the answer it teaches.

rows: `lease(2)`; another thread waits in `lease(3)` and is interrupted

cases.says: Leasing and giving back several buffers moves the free count down and up by that many.
A lease that waits for more buffers than are free holds none of them while it waits.
A tryLease that cannot get every buffer it asked for takes none and returns false.
A lease interrupted while it waits leaves with InterruptedException and takes nothing.

concepts: acquire(n) and tryAcquire(n) take all n permits together or none, so a waiter never holds a partial set that others need.
An InterruptedException from acquire is passed on or the interrupt flag restored, never swallowed, and the interrupted acquire holds nothing.
